source.title: Reinforcement Learning Towards Broadly and Persistently Beneficial Models
source.authors: Akshay V. Jagadeesh; Rahul K. Arora; Khaled Saab; Ali Malik; M. Trofimov; Foivos Tsimpourlas; Johannes Heidecke; Karan Singhal

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. Some figures are flattened in the text extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own tests of alignment performance under harmful persona prompting and harmful fine-tuning, which are conceptually related to safety persistence, but it does not test the specific behaviors or mechanisms named in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper measures alignment scores after harmful medical fine-tuning and under persona prompts, rather than harmful-request compliance or refusal rates after the claimed small-data fine-tuning and opening-token interventions. The aggregate refusal-rate findings are also reported, but they are not rates of harmful compliance after such interventions. Figure 6's per-evaluation results are described qualitatively; the text reports aggregate prompt-condition scores, which are recorded below.
record.test_reason: The study cites Qi et al. (2025) only in passing. Its persistence experiments fine-tune on bad medical advice and use persona prompt prefixes. It scores the results with alignment and health evaluations (HealthBench, emergent-misalignment questions, Model Spec compliance). It does not measure harmful-request compliance or refusal after small harmful or benign fine-tuning, per-token KL, prefill, suffix or decoding attacks, parameter localization, causes of shallowness, or token-deepening training. The fine-tuning is deliberate bad-advice training scored on alignment scores, which is an emergent-misalignment construct rather than V1's harmful-request compliance. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that beneficial-trait RL broadly improves out-of-distribution alignment and resists harmful persona steering while keeping helpful steerability. They also report reduced degradation after harmful medical fine-tuning, which they call preliminary. That fine-tuning comparison does not isolate trait RL from high-compute RL generally.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses reinforcement learning on beneficial-trait data and separately tests harmful medical fine-tuning and persona prompts. It does not use the cited studies' small harmful/benign fine-tuning, token-position KL, compliant-opening, suffix, or decoding interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different effects for harmful versus helpful persona prompts, and different degradation across health and broader alignment evaluations. Harmful fine-tuning causes larger declines for the pre-RL baseline than for the beneficial-trait RL model.

fits_no_version.finding: After fine-tuning on bad medical advice, the pre-RL baseline drops 0.27–0.46 on non-health alignment evaluations. The beneficial-trait RL model drops only 0.07–0.16. Health evaluations drop similarly for both (0.30–0.35 vs 0.21–0.31). The comparison uses a pre-RL rather than a compute-matched baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RL on beneficial traits (or high-compute RL generally) reduces emergent misalignment generalization from narrow harmful fine-tuning, as measured by alignment scores.

fits_no_version.finding: Harmful persona prefixes cut the average alignment score by 0.251 (baseline) vs 0.119 (trait RL). Helpful-persona gains are similar for both models (difference +0.0045, CI [-0.016, +0.025]).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Beneficial-trait RL selectively reduces harmful persona steerability while preserving helpful steerability.

fits_no_version.finding: Trait RL raises refusal rates: 13.2% to 23.9% on the alignment suite and 1.5% to 2.7% in everyday chat.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Alignment-focused RL modestly increases refusals, including in ordinary chat.

record.problems: The authors describe the harmful-fine-tuning evidence as preliminary, note that it uses a pre-RL rather than compute-matched standard-RL baseline, and call for more models, objectives, and evaluations. The prompt-persistence results summarize five evaluations and do not test the specific bypass methods in the claim. Several per-evaluation values appear only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows left out. Per-evaluation Figure 6 results are not separately extracted because the text gives aggregate condition values and qualitative descriptions rather than textual per-evaluation numbers.

untested.parts: Harmful-request compliance or refusal after a few to a few hundred harmful examples. The bad-medical-advice fine-tuning is scored only on alignment and health scores, and dataset size is not stated.
Benign fine-tuning effects on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Prefilling, adversarial suffixes and decoding changes. Persona prefixes are a system-prompt style steer, and no refusal-bypass rate is reported.
Localization of safety in weights or ranks.
Training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens.

missing.what: Disallowed mental-health persona results are not recorded: baseline 0.395 to 0.184, trait RL 0.455 to about 0.423. The degradation difference is +0.178 (95% CI [+0.069, +0.287]).

record.verdict_notes: An OpenAI study on frontier-scale internal models. The harmful fine-tuning is an emergent-misalignment setup and does not probe refusal-based shallow safety. Per-evaluation Figure 6 deltas appear only in the figure.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure harmful-request compliance or refusal removal after fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred harmful examples.
Does not test ordinary or carefully chosen benign instruction fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Does not measure per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Tests harmful persona prompts, but not compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes, and does not report harmful completion rates.
Does not localize safety behavior to weights, parameters, or ranks.
Does not test why safety is shallow or whether data or training objectives produce first-token concentration.
Does not test training intended to spread safety beyond initial response tokens.
